candidate: Daria Wrubel — Berkeley City Council D1
org_research: The California Working Families Party is a coalition of more than 30 grassroots organizations and labor unions with roughly 100,000 members, organized through regional chapters including the Bay Area, and governed in part by regional committees whose member representatives are elected by dues-paying members and vote in the endorsement process. Its stated priorities are economic justice, environmental protection, community safety, and countering corporate power; it claims a policy win banning AI-enabled price fixing. The party emphasizes co-governing — treating an endorsement as an ongoing accountability relationship — and asks candidates to pledge refusal of contributions from oil, law enforcement, real estate, charter school, and corporate PAC sources. This form is a combined statewide and local questionnaire, and roughly a third of its questions concern state legislative or ballot authority a city councilmember does not hold; the form's own preamble acknowledges that offices differ in power.

questions.analysis:
Asks for three concrete first-term initiatives. Each plank here names an instrument the office controls, and each has a documented Berkeley record behind it.

SURVEILLANCE. On May 7, 2026 Council severed the Flock package: it declined to execute the full agreement 8-1, then extended the automated license plate reader contract twelve months for up to $200,000 on a 5-4 vote, with Bartlett, Tregub, Lunaparra and Mayor Ishii opposed and the District 1 incumbent in the majority. It took no action on the Peace and Justice Commission's recommendation to cancel. The renewal lapses inside the next Council term. Two precision points matter. First, Berkeley has no facial recognition (prohibited by Ordinance 7,676-N.S.), no gunshot detection, no predictive policing, and the Police Department owns no drones — the phrase 'AI-powered cameras' does not describe anything Berkeley operates, and the City's own 156-page package uses the words 'AI' or 'machine learning' exactly once, in a prohibition. Say automated license plate readers. Second, the strongest fact is Berkeley's own: BPD's audit found outside agencies entering 'ICE' once and 'CBP' twice as the stated reason for searching statewide ALPR data that included Berkeley's, and BPD declined to find a violation.

POLICE TRANSPARENCY. The oversight body is the Police Accountability Board with an Office of the Director of Police Accountability, created by Measure II in 2020 under Charter Article XVIII section 125. It is not a 'Department of Police Accountability' — that is San Francisco's. The Charter already entitles the Board to records without redaction within ten business days and gives it subpoena power, yet two members resigned in January 2026 citing a pattern of reversals and describing years spent fighting for Charter-mandated access; Council dismissed the Director 8-0 in February; and the adopted budget cuts the office from six positions to four. BPD writes its own surveillance reports, and the November 2025 annual report was published without advance notice to the Board. The clean mechanism already exists in Berkeley law: BMC Chapter 2.100, adopted January 2026, requires Board review of BPD's annual equipment report and forces BPD to stop using equipment if Council does not act on a revocation recommendation within four meetings. BMC Chapter 2.99, which governs surveillance reporting, gives the Board no such role. Extending the 2.100 model to 2.99 is a specific, drafted-from-existing-text ask.

HARRISON STREET. The encampment is in District 1 and was still occupied as of the City's June 10, 2026 health update. Berkeley ran the precedent at 742 Grayson Street from 2021 to 2022, serving people displaced from the 8th and Harrison RV encampments; it closed on a lease expiry, not performance. Council already passed a referral in May 2025 seeking sites able to relocate an entire encampment to preserve a community, and staff declined to recommend funding one. Note the funding ambiguity: Alameda County's Measure W is the 2020 sales tax the County controls, distinct from Berkeley's own Measure W transfer tax. The County's acquisition and preservation round had not been released as of July 2026.

TOPA. Berkeley never took an up-or-down vote. On September 30, 2024 a motion to refer the ordinance for fiscal analysis failed 3-6, and a substitute motion to study a program modeled on San Francisco's COPA carried 6-3. The District 1 incumbent voted no on both. That referral is ranked 34th of 39 on the prioritized list adopted in February 2026, its sponsor field is blank, and no staff report has ever come back. The evidence has to be handled carefully: in Washington DC across 2006 to 2020, tenants actually purchased 2.1 percent of units that went through TOPA while 49 percent were assigned to developers. What TOPA reliably produces is leverage rather than tenant ownership — roughly 40 percent of assigned units had affordability preserved or added and 78 percent were renovated — at a measured cost of about 5.3 months of additional time to sell. Berkeley's binding constraint is not the legal right but capital and capacity: the Small Sites Program holds $3.8 million, Measure O and Measure A1 are effectively committed, and the City approved its third Small Sites project since 2017 in 2024 after receiving a single proposal. Two nonprofits have acquired four occupied buildings in Berkeley in nine years.

verification.source: Portland State University Homelessness Research & Action Collaborative, Alternative Shelter Evaluation Report (Multnomah County); Los Angeles City Controller, Pathways to Permanent Housing

verification.source: CNHED, Sustaining Affordability, Council-commissioned analysis of DHCD data for Washington DC, 2006-2020
verification.note: Of 37,471 units sold following a TOPA notice, tenant associations registered on 23,266, 18,399 were assigned to a developer, and tenants purchased 771 — 2.1 percent. verification.source: D.C. Law 22-120 (2018); RENTAL Amendment Act of 2025, D.C. Law 26-80

The tenant-support provisions enacted alongside — tenant support providers, a qualified purchaser program, a transparency portal — are subject to appropriation, unfunded, and legally inoperative.

verification.source: City of Berkeley Housing Element Annual Progress Report; Small Sites Program guidelines; Measure O and Measure A1 commitment reports
verification.note: The Small Sites Program holds about $3.8 million and is the only live acquisition money; Measure O has issued $76.7 million of $135 million and reports it all committed or reserved; Measure A1 is roughly 97 percent committed; the state Foreclosure Intervention Housing Preservation Program reverted $236.5 million without making a single award. Berkeley approved its third Small Sites project since 2017 in 2024, after receiving one proposal. Two nonprofits have acquired four occupied buildings in Berkeley in nine years, against roughly 245 multifamily sales annually.

verification.source: San Francisco COPA program page and MOHCD Program Rules; SF Administrative Code Chapter 41B

verification.claim: San Francisco's COPA gives nonprofits a workable window to act
verification.source: SF Ordinance 79-19 adding Administrative Code Chapter 41B, sections 41B.6 and 41B.7
verification.note: Qualified nonprofits get five calendar days to express interest, twenty-five more to make an offer, and sixty days of due diligence. Berkeley's own 2022 analysis concluded San Francisco's timeframes 'are insufficient' and 'have resulted in lost opportunities.' Rights run to nonprofits only; there is no tenant-ownership pathway.

questions.question: Do you support repealing the Ellis Act?
questions.analysis: Repealing the Ellis Act requires state legislation; a councilmember can advocate but not vote. Berkeley already regulates Ellis withdrawals as far as state law permits, under BMC Chapter 13.77: relocation payments of $19,413 per household plus $6,471 for low-income, elderly, disabled, or long-tenancy households as of January 1, 2026; a ten-year right of first refusal for displaced tenants; punitive damages if a unit is re-rented within two years; a rent rollback if re-rented within five years; and a ten-year bar on condominium conversion. Withdrawal volume is low by regional standards — 508 units across 172 filings since July 1986 — which means the local answer is about closing a remaining escape hatch rather than responding to a crisis.

questions.question: Do you support repealing Costa Hawkins?
questions.analysis: Repealing Costa-Hawkins requires state action, but for Berkeley the consequences are unusually concrete: the municipal code already contains dormant standby provisions written to activate on repeal. BMC 13.76.100(D) restores a rent ceiling at the most recent lawfully established rent if state law stops mandating that landlords set initial rents, which ends vacancy decontrol going forward. BMC 13.76.050(B)(1) converts the permanent post-June-1980 new-construction exemption into a rolling fifteen-year exemption. BMC 13.76.050(B)(2) self-terminates by its own terms, bringing single-family homes and condominiums under full coverage. Roughly 20,000 Berkeley units currently have regulated rents. The candidate can therefore answer this question with specific local mechanics rather than general support.

questions.question: Do you support a fully funded Right to Counsel program for renters in your jurisdiction?
questions.analysis: The question's premise does not hold for this jurisdiction. Berkeley has no codified right to counsel: exact-phrase searches of the municipal code, charter, and ordinances for 'right to counsel', 'legal defense', and 'eviction defense' return no match. What Berkeley has instead is contracted eviction-defense legal services funded through Measure U1 — roughly $800,000 a year split between the East Bay Community Law Center and the Eviction Defense Center — plus the separate Housing Retention Program, which grants up to $10,000 toward rent arrears for households at or below 50% AMI and funds no legal representation at all. questions.question: Do you support policies that would ban the use of price setting algorithms in the housing market? (ie. Realpage)
questions.analysis: Berkeley has already legislated here, and the legislative history matters more than the headline. Ordinance 7,956-N.S. added BMC Chapter 13.63 and was adopted March 25, 2025, effective April 24, 2025. RealPage sued in RealPage, Inc. v. City of Berkeley (N.D. Cal. 3:25-cv-03004-JSC) on First Amendment grounds; the City agreed not to enforce pending the preliminary-injunction motion and Ordinance 7,974-N.S. suspended the effective date. Ordinance 7,992-N.S., adopted December 2, 2025, deleted the suspension and substantially narrowed the prohibition: 'competitor data' now reaches only information not available to the general public, about properties the landlord does not own or manage, and less than 90 days old, with carve-outs for appraisal, project financing, and machine-learning model training. The narrowed ordinance is in force, carrying penalties up to $1,000 per violation per unit per month plus a private right of action. Describing Berkeley as having banned RealPage without that history would overstate what survived. Note also that the California WFP claims banning AI-enabled price fixing as one of its own policy wins, so this is a question the organization follows closely.

questions.question: Will you invest in non-police emergency response systems?
questions.analysis: Berkeley has moved backwards on this within the last two months, and the answer must reflect that. The Specialized Care Unit — a three-person team of a peer support specialist, an EMT, and a clinician, operated under contract by Bonita House and reached at its own phone line — ran from September 5, 2023 to May 2025 and is recorded as complete in the City's Reimagining Public Safety status update. It was funded entirely with one-time money: $4.75 million in ARPA, a $536,500 DHCS grant that expired June 30, 2025, and $68,000 in MHSA, with the City Manager's April 2025 memo stating plainly that there is no recurring funding. Then the budget adopted June 23, 2026 eliminated the 2.6 remaining FTE of the Mobile Crisis Team, described in the budget document as the last General Fund–funded mental health crisis response positions, with responsibility for wellness checks and psychiatric emergencies shifting solely to the Police Department. BerkDOT was never created: the July 2020 action was a referral to the City Manager, it is classified as paused and defunded at Tier 3, and traffic and parking enforcement both remain inside the Police Department. questions.analysis: This is a multiple-choice question where Berkeley's actual ordinance supports the strongest option without qualification. Ordinance 7,984-N.S., adding BMC Chapter 13.114, was adopted on second reading September 30, 2025 and contains no criminal offense carve-out — no serious or violent felony list, no Penal Code 1192.7 or 667.5 exception. Its only exceptions are consent, service provision, and what state or federal law compels. This matters because state law leaves that discretion open: Government Code 7282.5 permits, but does not require, cooperation for a long list of offenses, and expressly conditions it on not violating local policy. Berkeley closes that door. Police Department Policy 415 reproduces the ordinance and states that members 'shall not transfer an individual to immigration authorities.' Berkeley also goes beyond SB 54 by binding every City agency and contractor, requiring written reporting of every ICE request to Council within ten business days, and restricting consent searches of non-public City property. Two cautions: a January 2025 council report miscites the 1986 sanctuary resolution number, and Policy 415.7.5 retains residual template language about reporting transfers that contradicts the flat prohibition — not an operative carve-out, but a hostile questioner could point at it.

questions.question: What distinguishes you as a Working Families Party candidate from your opponents?
questions.analysis: A comparative question. The distinction WFP looks for is structural — funding sources, base of support, and accountability to organizations — rather than differences in stated positions, since in Berkeley most candidates will state similar ones. The answer runs on three claims, each independently checkable. First, the surveillance contract: on May 7, 2026 the Council declined the Peace and Justice Commission's recommendation to cancel Berkeley's Flock Safety contracts, rejected a roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones, and adopted Resolution 72,254-N.S. renewing the automated license plate reader contract twelve months for up to $200,000 — so the expansion was stopped and the underlying contract was not, and the renewal lapses inside the next Council term. Second, the sanctuary claim: Berkeley's ordinance, BMC Chapter 13.114, contains no criminal carve-out and binds every City agency and contractor, which is what makes a procurement decision a sanctuary question rather than a separate one. Third, campaign structure: BMC 2.12.440 already bars corporate, business-entity, and union contributions to any Berkeley candidate, and the public financing program caps contributions at $60 and bars PAC money outright, so the independence claim is a legal fact about the campaign rather than a promise. Note that another Berkeley candidate has run on ending the Flock contract, so this is a shared position in the field and the distinction has to rest on more than holding it.
